s1.explanation: The unit responds to a close-up, front-facing dog face, mostly when it fills much of the photo and the dark eyes and nose stand out as distinct spots on a light (white, cream or grey) furred face. It responds most to light fluffy small dogs and to wolf, kuvasz and Appenzeller faces looking at the camera. It is weak when the dog is small or far away in the scene, seen whole-body at a distance, or when the face is uniformly reddish-brown, so the eyes and nose have little contrast. Compared with the similar units, it prefers large, frontal, high-contrast faces over the dog's overall body, coat texture or distant views.

s2.explanation: The unit responds to the face and body of a light-colored (white, cream or pale tan) fluffy dog that fills much of the photo and faces the camera, with dark eyes and nose visible. It is strongest on close or medium shots of small white long-haired dogs such as Maltese, Westies and Dandie Dinmonts. Activity drops sharply when the dog is small in a wide scene (far-off kuvasz, dog in a show backdrop, dog on autumn leaves). It is also weaker for dark or wiry-coated dogs. Compared with the similar units, it stays high for close-up frontal faces even of non-terrier canids (wolf, corgi, close-up kuvasz). It is low when the dog is distant.

s3.explanation: The unit responds mostly to a large, close-up, front-facing dog face, especially one with light-colored (white or cream) fluffy fur and clearly visible dark eyes and nose. Activity is highest when the face fills much of the frame and looks toward the camera, whether the dog is a Maltese, a kuvasz head shot or a wolf. Activity drops sharply when the dog is small in a wide scene (a distant kuvasz in fog, a Leonberg or a Dandie standing full-body with a person) and is lower for dark reddish-brown wiry faces. Compared with similar units, this unit prefers close frontal face crops over full-body views.

real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to a large, close-up, front-facing dog face in which the dark eyes and nose stand out as distinct, high-contrast spots.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to a large, close-up dog face turned toward the camera, with the eyes and nose clearly visible; coat color and fur texture matter little.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to a large, close-up dog face looking toward the camera, with both eyes and the nose visible, regardless of fur color.

null_s1.explanation: The unit is active on dog-related photo classes (light fluffy small dogs, wolf, kuvasz, Appenzeller). Within those classes, none of the proposed visual features explains its activity: face size, frontal pose, fur color and eye/nose contrast all fail.

null_s2.explanation: The unit most likely responds to certain dog breeds at the class level, plausibly small light-coated long-haired breeds such as Maltese, Westies and Dandie Dinmonts. Within a breed, it does not track the dog filling the frame, facing the camera, a pale coat or fluffy fur.

null_s3.explanation: The unit seems to respond to dogs at the level of breed or class, mainly fluffy, long-coated dogs such as Maltese, kuvasz, Leonberg and Dandie Dinmont, with weaker responses to related canids such as wolves. How the dog is framed, how it is posed and its face color do not appear to matter.
